specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between the moment of a force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot

primer.text: Forces do more than push objects along in a straight line — they can also make them turn. A stiff door, a spanner and a playground see-saw all rotate about a fixed point when a force acts. This note names that turning effect, shows the clockwise and anticlockwise senses it can take, and builds the equation that measures it.

lessons.title: The moment of a force
sourceHeadings: An object rotating clockwise about a pivot
lessons.opening: Push a see-saw and it swings; twist a tap and it turns — forces can spin things as well as shove them. The spinning action a force produces about a fixed turning point is called a moment. This lesson pins down that idea and the two senses of rotation it can take.
keyPoints: A moment is the turning effect that a force gives about a pivot.
Everyday examples include see-saws, spanner handles, doors, cranes, screwdrivers, taps, wheelbarrows and scissors.
Forces can make an object rotate around a fixed pivot, turning either clockwise or anticlockwise.
A force applied to one side of a pivot makes the object rotate.
The direction of turning is judged against the way a clock's hands travel.

low.restatement: A moment is the turning effect a force has about a pivot; the spin it produces runs clockwise or anticlockwise.
low.analogy: A playground roundabout: where you lean and push decides which way it sweeps around its central post.
low.examPointer: When a question asks for the direction of turning, answer with the exact sense — clockwise or anticlockwise — not a bare 'it rotates'.

medium.restatement: The pivot is the fixed point the object swings about; a force pushing on just one side of it sets the whole object rotating in one definite sense.
medium.analogy: Treat a clock face as the referee: a sweep from the 12 towards the 3 is clockwise, the reverse sweep anticlockwise.
medium.examPointer: Even before any calculation, label the sense of rotation on the diagram — examiners expect the clock comparison.

check.stem: A moment is best described as:

options.text: The amount of matter packed into an object
options.explanation: That is mass, a different quantity entirely.

options.text: The speed at which an object spins
options.explanation: A moment sizes a turning effect; it is not a rotation speed.

options.text: The turning effect a force produces about a pivot
options.explanation: That is the definition of record.

options.text: A force stored inside an object
options.explanation: Nothing is stored; the moment describes the turning action of an applied force.

check.stem: A rotation is described as clockwise when it turns in the same direction as:

options.explanation: The clock face is the reference: matching its hands means clockwise.

options.text: A planet's orbit around the Sun
options.explanation: The comparison of record is a clock, not planetary motion.
A pendulum sweeps both ways, so it cannot define one sense.
A downward force can turn an object either way, depending on where it acts.

check.stem: Which everyday action involves a moment producing rotation?

options.text: Sliding a box along the floor
options.explanation: Straight-line sliding involves no turn about a pivot.

options.text: Squeezing a sponge between your palms
options.explanation: A squeeze deforms the sponge without rotating it about a pivot.

options.text: A picture hanging still on a wall
options.explanation: Nothing turns, so no moment acts.

options.text: Twisting a tap on and off
options.explanation: The tap head rotates about its spindle — a standard moment example.

check.stem: A force is applied on just one side of a pivot. What is the result?

options.explanation: A one-sided push cannot balance; it turns the object.

options.text: The object rotates about the pivot
options.explanation: A force acting to one side of a pivot produces turning.

options.text: The object slides away without any turning
options.explanation: An off-centre force turns the object as well as moving it.

options.text: The pivot moves across to meet the force
options.explanation: The pivot is fixed — that is what makes the rotation well defined.

check.stem: A door swings open. Which part acts as its fixed pivot?

options.explanation: That is where the force is applied, not the turning point.
The floor supports the door but is not the rotation's fixed point.
The hinge is the fixed pivot about which the door turns.
The handle carries the push; it is not the fixed turning point.

check.stem: State what is meant by a moment.
check.modelAnswer: A moment is the turning effect that a force produces about a pivot.

check.stem: Give two everyday examples of rotation caused by a moment.
check.modelAnswer: Any two of: a child on a see-saw, a spanner turning a nut, a door opening, a crane lifting supplies, a screwdriver opening a paint tin, a tap twisted on, a wheelbarrow lifted, or scissors cutting.

check.stem: Explain why the rotation caused by a moment is labelled either clockwise or anticlockwise, and what reference settles the choice.
check.modelAnswer: The object spins about a fixed pivot, so its parts all sweep the same way round that point. Comparing the sweep with the hands of a clock gives the label: matching them is clockwise, the reverse is anticlockwise.

check.stem: A learner says 'the hinge is the moment of the door'. Rewrite the sentence using the correct terms.
check.modelAnswer: The hinge is the pivot — the fixed point the door turns about — while the moment is the turning effect the applied force produces.

lessons.title: Calculating moments with M = F × d
sourceHeadings: The moment of a force exerted on a spanner
Forces required to open a door
lessons.opening: Sizing a turning effect takes one multiplication. The moment equals the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the pivot — the straight-across gap to that turning point — and it is measured in newton metres. Step back from the hinge and a lighter push opens the same door.
keyPoints: The size of a moment is M = F × d: force times perpendicular distance from the pivot.
M is the moment in newton metres (N m), F the force in newtons (N), and d the perpendicular distance in metres (m).
The force should act perpendicular to the distance that separates it from the pivot — on a horizontal beam, up or down forces create moments.
Pushing farther from the pivot needs less force — pushing a door near the hinge is hard, at the handle it is easy.
Moments may be quoted in newton centimetres when the distance is in centimetres; convert distances to metres unless the question names a unit.

low.restatement: Multiply the force by its perpendicular distance from the pivot and you have the moment: M = F × d.
low.analogy: A longer spanner arm is a force multiplier: the same hand grip swings a stiffer nut because the extra reach does part of the work.
low.examPointer: Watch the units: force in newtons and distance in metres give a moment in newton metres (N m).

medium.restatement: M = F × d runs both ways: divide the moment by the distance to recover the force, or by the force to recover the distance.
medium.analogy: Reach is a discount on effort: every extra metre from the pivot buys the same turn for fewer newtons.
medium.examPointer: If the question gives centimetres and names no unit for the answer, convert the distance to metres before multiplying — newton metres is the default.

check.stem: A force of 10 N acts 0.50 m from a pivot, at right angles to the distance. The moment is:

options.explanation: That divides the distance by the force.
That divides the force by the distance instead of multiplying.
That adds the two values.

check.stem: With F in newtons and d in metres, the moment M comes out in:

options.explanation: Newtons measure the force alone, not force times distance.
Metres measure the distance alone.
That would divide force by distance; the relationship multiplies them.
Force (N) times distance (m) gives the moment unit N m.

check.stem: On a horizontal beam, which forces create a moment about a point on the beam?

options.text: Forces pointing straight up or down
options.explanation: Up or down forces cut across a horizontal beam — exactly the perpendicular case.

options.text: Forces directed along the beam itself
options.explanation: A push straight along the beam has no perpendicular separation, so it produces no turning.

options.text: Whichever force on the beam is largest
options.explanation: Size alone never decides; the direction relative to the distance matters.
The moment equation applies when the force acts across the perpendicular gap to the pivot, not along it.

check.stem: Pushing a door open at the handle, far from the hinges, is easier than pushing next to them because:

options.text: The handle multiplies the force you exert
options.explanation: The handle adds no force; it adds distance from the pivot.

options.text: The door becomes lighter farther from the hinges
options.explanation: The door's weight never changes with where you push.

options.text: The greater distance from the pivot lets a smaller force supply the moment
options.explanation: A longer distance from the pivot decreases the force needed for the same turning effect.

options.text: The hinges grip more loosely near the handle
options.explanation: Hinge conditions are identical; only the geometry of the push changes.

check.stem: A moment of 30 N m is produced by a 5 N force. The force's perpendicular distance from the pivot is:

options.explanation: That multiplies instead of dividing.
That divides the force by the moment, upside down.
That adds the two values.

check.stem: State the equation for the moment of a force and give the unit of the moment.
check.modelAnswer: M = F × d, where M is the moment in newton metres (N m), F is the force in newtons (N) and d is the perpendicular distance in metres (m).

check.stem: Why should distances be converted into metres before calculating a moment, and what units result?
check.modelAnswer: Working in metres keeps the standard units, so the moment comes out in newton metres (N m); leaving the distance in centimetres would give newton centimetres instead. Convert unless the question names a unit.

check.stem: Explain why increasing the distance from the pivot decreases the force needed for a given moment.
check.modelAnswer: In M = F × d, the moment required for the task is fixed, so force and distance trade off inversely: any increase in d lets F fall by the same factor. Reaching farther from the pivot therefore buys the same turning effect with a smaller force.

check.stem: A spanner pushes with a 15 N force at 0.40 m from the nut — the pivot. Compute the moment, then state the force needed if the grip moves out to 0.50 m for the same moment.
check.modelAnswer: M = 15 × 0.40 = 6.0 N m. At 0.50 m: F = 6.0 ÷ 0.50 = 12 N — farther from the pivot, the needed force drops to 12 N.

glossary.definition: The turning effect that a force produces about a pivot.
The fixed point about which an object rotates when a force turns it.
Turning the same way as the hands of a clock.
Turning the opposite way to the hands of a clock.
The unit of moment: one newton acting one metre from the pivot, written N m.
The straight-across gap from the pivot to the force's line, the d in M = F × d.
